 IAF Nears Deal For 6 Converted Pre-Owned Boeing-767 Tankers Under HAL-IAI Tie-Up; Deliveries Expected Over 2028–30
 Thread starter 
 Thread starter 
 Chandresh 
 Start date 
 Start date

 Replies: 8
The Indian Air Force (IAF) is on the verge of sealing a highly anticipated agreement to acquire six Multi-Mission Tanker Transport (MMTT) aircraft.
Once the final contract is signed, the induction of these crucial assets is projected to occur in phases between 2028 and 2030.
Valued at approximately ₹8,000 to ₹9,000 crore—roughly $1.1 billion—this major procurement aims to substantially upgrade the military's mid-air refuelling capacities.
The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) had previously granted its initial clearance for the capital expenditure, paving the way for the concluding contract negotiations.
This impending purchase is a vital measure to resolve a severe operational gap for the armed forces.
At present, India relies on a limited squadron of six Soviet-era Ilyushin IL-78 mid-air refuellers, which have been plagued by poor serviceability rates and heavy maintenance burdens over the past few years.
To execute this project, the plan involves procuring civilian, pre-owned Boeing-767 passenger jets and modifying them into sophisticated military tankers.
Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), which holds extensive global experience in converting civilian airliners into military tankers, will partner with Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) to carry out the complex engineering and modification work in India.
These newly modified aircraft will be equipped for a variety of tasks that go beyond simply dispensing fuel in mid-air.
Aside from boosting the flight times and combat radius of fighter jets, the Boeing-767 MMTTs can be rapidly adapted to transport military personnel, ferry heavy cargo, and conduct strategic airlift missions, thereby giving the IAF immense operational versatility during both peacetime logistics and active conflicts.
This strategy marks a significant departure from the government's previous attempts to buy brand-new refuellers. In earlier bidding contests, the European Airbus A330 MRTT emerged as the technically preferred choice, but the purchase was repeatedly shelved due to prohibitive pricing.
Opting to convert existing Boeing-767 airframes is widely considered a highly cost-effective alternative, offering the desired military capabilities at a fraction of the initial purchase and long-term maintenance costs.
Once inducted, the MMTT fleet will significantly amplify the striking range of India's frontline combat jets, such as the Dassault Rafale and the Sukhoi Su-30MKI.
Enhanced aerial refuelling will permit Indian fighter pilots to stay in the sky for extended durations and launch deep-penetration strikes across vast distances without the need to land at forward airbases.
The tanker programme also strongly supports the nation's push for self-reliance in the defence manufacturing sector.
Under the agreement, HAL and other domestic private enterprises will take on a major share of the structural integration, maintenance, and lifetime technical support.
This collaborative model aims to cut down dependence on foreign suppliers while upgrading India's indigenous aerospace industry.
Defence experts view this procurement as an essential milestone, as reliable aerial refuelling remains a cornerstone for projecting air dominance, sustaining long-range missions, and securing India's strategic interests across the region.

 Yes the Sukhoi can carry a lot of fuel, but then a) it guzzles a lot and b) that limits the ordinance it can carry for A-G work. So tanker support is preferable especially if you want him loaded for bear. Same with the others. External fuel tanks use up external stations limiting weapon carriage.
For those who want to arrive at an ideal number of tankers for IAF, here is a hint. Check the number of tankers the USAF operates. Then work out the ratio of combat ac to tanlers. Now comes the tricky part. Now you need to extrapolate the USAF committments vs IAF committments. Keep in mind that the IAF is not an expeditionary force, but essentially has the same two front prep as the US albeit on a smaller scale.
Do the math and you would come very close to what the IAF thinks it needs.
I wont share the actual thought process or the numbers, but if people do the math, you will get a good idea.
